**Finding 2: Permanent job stall / loss when no reaper exists** **Steelman:** PostgreSQL's MVCC guarantees that a crashed worker's uncommitted transaction is rolled back, automatically releasing its locks and making the job visible again. In the commit-then-work pattern (the common case to avoid long-running transactions), the job is already durably 'processing' with no lock held. PostgreSQL has no mechanism to roll back a committed UPDATE because the issuing process has since died. ## Finding 3: Redis Eviction Under Memory Pressure Silently Removes Keys Before 24-Hour TTL **Steelman:** The key has a 24-hour TTL, so Redis will not evict it prematurely. **Weakness:** TTL guarantees expiry *no earlier than* the set duration only when Redis has headroom. When `maxmemory` is configured (as is standard in managed Redis services to prevent OOM kills) and the eviction policy is `volatile-lru`, `volatile-lfu`, or `allkeys-lru`, Redis evicts keys — including those with unexpired TTLs — to free space. A high-write-volume period (e.g., a sale event) can flush idempotency keys that are only a few minutes old. All retry requests for those payments within the still-valid 24-hour business window will see a clean miss and re-charge. Autovacuum is throttled by `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay` and `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit`; if the table is hot, it backs off. ## Finding 2 — Async Replication Guarantees RPO > 0; Failover Loses Messages **Steelman:** Two-datacenter deployments provide disaster recovery; if DC1 fails, consumers switch to DC2 and processing continues. **Weakness:** Asynchronous replication (the only practical option at WAN latencies) has a nonzero replication lag. Any messages produced and committed in DC1 but not yet consumed by the replicator are lost on DC1 failure. When DC1 later recovers, those messages still exist in DC1's logs, but consumer offsets in DC2 have already advanced past them.
